title: Souls return
hook: many kabbalists taught reincarnation; not all Jews hold this view

segments.voice: Yesterday, repairing the world: a phrase that ran from the Mishnah to a food-drive sign. Your line was repair the world. Which bigger repair did your small act belong to? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-seven.

"One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh; and the earth abideth for ever." That's Ecclesiastes, watching the parade go by. People arrive, people leave, the ground stays put. But the line leaves a question hanging. The earth abides. What about the soul that walked on it for one generation? Jewish tradition holds more than one answer to that, side by side. Today's word belongs to the kabbalists, and it isn't the only Jewish answer. Today's word.
screen: `ONE GENERATION PASSES.` → `THE EARTH ABIDES.` → `AND THE SOUL?`

segments.voice: Gilgul. In full, gilgul neshamot, often put into English as the cycling of souls. Turn it four ways. First, what it says. Kabbalists taught that a soul can come back to this world in another life, in another body. The Zohar speaks of it, and Chaim Vital gathered Luria's teachings on it into a book called Sha'ar ha-Gilgulim, the Gate of Reincarnations. Second, why a soul returns. The reason these teachers give is repair, tikkun, the thread from the last few days. A soul comes back to finish a commandment it missed, to mend a wrong, to complete its share of gathering the sparks. Not a punishment so much as unfinished work. Third, the other voices. Not all Jews hold this view. The Torah doesn't spell it out. Saadia Gaon, a medieval Jewish philosopher, argued against it, and other thinkers set it aside. Jewish tradition also speaks, in its own words, of the soul returning to God, of the world to come, and of the resurrection of the dead. Ecclesiastes says simply that the spirit returneth unto God who gave it. These views live in the same tradition, and people who hold them pray side by side. Fourth, what they share. Whether a soul returns, rests with God, or waits for the world to come, none of these answers treats a life as a sealed box. What a person does spills past them: a name given in memory, a kindness taught to a child, a promise kept by a grandchild. Some readers hear gilgul as that same idea, told in the language of souls.
screen: `A SOUL CAN RETURN.` · `TO FINISH ITS REPAIR.` · `NOT ALL JEWS HOLD THIS.` · `A LIFE IS NOT A SEALED BOX.` · then, large: `SOULS CONTINUE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think about what continues after us. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who has died whose ways still show up in you. A phrase you say. A recipe. The way you fold a towel. A kindness you learned from them. If no one comes to mind, choose a teacher or an author. Hold that thread for a while. Then turn it forward. What of yours might carry on after you? A habit, a story, the way you treat people. No need to decide anything. Just notice the threads, running back and running forward. The bell holds the time.
Gilgul. The return of a soul to another life, taught by kabbalists as a way to finish its repair, and not held by all Jews. Today's word.
Your line: souls continue. Today, do one thing the way someone who's gone used to do it, and let it carry on through you. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Gilgul is taught in Kabbalah and Hasidic thought, especially through Chaim Vital's Sha'ar ha-Gilgulim; other Jews focus instead on the soul's return to God, the world to come, and the resurrection of the dead.
